## Chapter Summary

Data preparation is the most time-consuming and arguably the most important stage of any accounting analytics project. Raw accounting data almost always contains problems that must be resolved before analysis can produce reliable results. Extra spaces, inconsistent capitalization, and embedded characters in text fields cause matching failures. Transaction dates must be decomposed into fiscal periods before time-based analysis is possible. Data spread across multiple tables must be merged into a single dataset before questions that span those tables can be answered. Missing values and duplicate records must be identified and handled with professional judgment. This chapter taught the Excel tools that address each of these challenges using the Charles River data.

Text functions including TRIM, CLEAN, SUBSTITUTE, UPPER, LOWER, PROPER, LEFT, RIGHT, MID, LEN, and FIND transform qualitative fields into consistent formats that support accurate matching, grouping, and reporting. These functions apply to item names, customer names, supplier names, and any other text field that participates in lookups or aggregations. The functions create new cleaned values in formula cells while preserving the original data, which allows the accountant to verify the transformation before replacing the source values.

Date functions including YEAR, MONTH, DAY, and ROUNDUP extract time-period components from transaction dates such as the SalesOrder OrderDate and the SalesInvoice InvoiceDate. Fiscal quarter assignment formulas map each date to the correct quarter based on the organization's fiscal year start month. Date arithmetic calculates the number of days between events, which supports aging analysis, fulfillment time calculations, and other period-based measures.

Lookup functions merge data from multiple Charles River tables by matching on shared identifiers. VLOOKUP provides basic lookup capability but is limited to searching the leftmost column. XLOOKUP offers greater flexibility by allowing the analyst to specify both the lookup column and the return column independently, and it includes built-in error handling. INDEX/MATCH provides the same flexibility as XLOOKUP and works in all Excel versions. Each function serves the same fundamental purpose of connecting related data across tables, which is the Excel equivalent of the SQL joins taught in Chapter 10. Because the SalesOrderLine table stores SalesOrderID rather than CustomerID, retrieving a customer name from a sales line requires a nested lookup that first finds the CustomerID from the order and then finds the name from the customer master.

Missing values are detected using ISBLANK and COUNTBLANK and handled using IF formulas that substitute appropriate default labels, as with orders that have no shipment date because they have not yet shipped. Duplicate records are detected using COUNTIFS and can be removed using Excel's Remove Duplicates tool, but removal should always follow manual review and documentation, particularly in audit contexts where the completeness of the population is critical. Power Query provides a structured, documented, and repeatable alternative to formula-based preparation. Each transformation step is recorded automatically and can be reviewed, edited, or rerun, and the merge operation combines tables on a matching key column as a single documented step. Power Query's repeatability makes it the preferred approach for any data preparation workflow that you will perform more than once, such as monthly or quarterly analytical procedures.
